sermon:
## Made, Not Random

*Genesis 1–2*

There is a kind of tiredness that no amount of sleep touches. It is the suspicion, lodged somewhere under the ribs, that you are an accident the universe will eventually correct. A friend of mine, an engineer, told me once that on the hardest nights he could not shake the math: a few decades of carbon arranged briefly into a man, then unarranged. He did not say it to be dramatic. He said it the way you report the weather. That is where Genesis begins to speak, not into a debate, but into that ache.

The first chapter does not argue. It declares. "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). Notice what the text refuses to do. It does not prove God. It does not flatter the reader. It opens with a working God ordering chaos into goodness, and it keeps a rhythm: He spoke, it was so, it was good. Light. Sky. Land and sea. Things that grow and swim and fly. Seven times the verdict falls, good, good, very good. The world is not neutral material waiting for us to assign it worth. It came already weighted with the approval of the One who made it.

**The pattern is purpose, not chance**

Read the six days slowly and you see craftsmanship, not collision. The first three days form the spaces. The second three fill them. Day and night, then sun and moon and stars. Sky and sea, then birds and fish. Dry land, then animals and at last a man and a woman. This is not the residue of an explosion. It is a house being built room by room, and then furnished, by Someone who intends to dwell in it. The ancient near east told its neighbors that the world was made from the corpse of a defeated god, that humanity was an afterthought to do the gods' chores. Genesis stands against all of it. The world is not violence. It is gift.

**You were made on purpose, in His image**

Then comes the sentence that should reorder how you see the person beside you and the one in the mirror. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). In the surrounding cultures, only the king bore the image of a god. Genesis democratizes the crown and lays it on every head. The dignity is not earned by intelligence, productivity, beauty, or use. It is conferred. In chapter two we watch it happen up close, God stooping to form a man from dust and breathing into him, planting a garden, calling it not good that the man should be alone, building a woman from his side. This is not mass production. It is the attention of a Father.

Here is where I have to implicate myself. I treat people as accidents all the time. The cashier who is slow, the man who cut me off, the difficult member of my own household, I assign them worth by their usefulness to me, which is exactly the lie Genesis was written to kill. If they bear the image, my contempt is a kind of vandalism. And so is my self-contempt. The voice that tells me I am a mistake is not humility. It is unbelief. It calls God a careless workman.

**The image restored in Christ**

The image cracked in the chapters ahead, but the New Testament names the One who carries it whole. Paul writes that Christ is "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). The same Word that spoke light into the dark took on dust and breath and walked among us, and by His death and rising He is making us new, conforming us back to the image we were made to bear. You are not an accident the universe will correct. You are a creature the Creator is determined to restore.

So the next time the old math returns on a sleepless night, the few decades of carbon, answer it with the older math. Spoken. Formed. Breathed into. Called very good before you had done a single thing to deserve it.

You bear the image you did not earn.

## The Day It Broke

*Genesis 3*

Ask a child why they did the thing they were told not to do, and watch the answer arrive before the words. The eyes go somewhere else. The story shifts. It was the other kid, it was already broken, I did not hear you. We learn the choreography of blame before we learn to spell. We did not invent it. We inherited it. Genesis 3 is the room where it was first performed.

The scene is quiet, almost domestic. A garden, a tree, a question. The serpent does not begin with an order. He begins with a doubt dressed as curiosity. "Did God actually say..." And then he edits God's words just enough to make God sound stingy, a withholder, a rule-maker hoarding something good. The woman corrects him, then adds to the prohibition herself, and the conversation is already off its footing. Notice that no one in this scene is hungry. The fruit is not survival. It is something else.

**Sin is not breaking a rule. It is refusing to be a creature.**

Hear the actual offer: "You will be like God, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5). That is the hook, and we keep swallowing it. The temptation was never mainly about a piece of fruit. It was about jurisdiction. It was the creature deciding to be the Creator, to set the terms, to define good and evil rather than receive them. To eat was to say: I will not live as a made thing under a good God. I will be my own god, on my own ground, by my own definition. Theologians have a word for this, and it is not a small one. It is the will to rule what you were made to receive.

This is why moralism never reaches deep enough. We treat sin as a list of broken rules and imagine that with enough effort we could shorten the list. But the rebellion underneath the rules is the refusal to be a creature at all, the grasp for a throne that was never ours. You can keep every commandment and still be running the original program, sitting in God's chair, auditing His goodness.

**The grasp always costs more than it promised**

They ate, and the serpent kept none of his promises. Their eyes were opened, yes, but to shame. The first thing the knowledge of good and evil produced was the desperate sewing of fig leaves and the instinct to hide from the One who used to walk with them in the cool of the day. Then the choreography begins. God asks, and the man blames the woman and, underneath her, God Himself: "the woman whom you gave to be with me." She blames the serpent. No one says the only honest sentence: I did this. The ground is cursed, the relationships fracture, the gate closes. Every grasp for the throne ends in exile from it.

I know this ground. I have stood in the cool of the day with my fig leaves stitched and ready, explaining to God why the thing was not really my fault, why my circumstances forced it, why I am the exception. I have done it from a pulpit. The serpent does not need me to deny God exists. He only needs me to keep editing what God said until obedience sounds like loss and self-rule sounds like freedom.

**The promise in the curse**

And yet into the wreckage God speaks a sentence aimed at the serpent: the offspring of the woman "shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15). The oldest promise in Scripture is buried in a curse. A child of the woman is coming who will take the serpent's strike in His heel and crush the serpent's skull in return. The day it broke, God already named the day it would be healed. On a hill outside Jerusalem, a heel was pierced through, and the head of the ancient grasp was crushed. The second Adam refused the very thing the first one seized. He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped. He received the cup His Father gave.

That is the only way back from the garden gate. Not a tighter grip. An open hand.

Every wrong began with one grasp.

## Judgment and the Ark

*Genesis 6–9*

We have made the flood a nursery. Pairs of smiling animals, a rainbow, a felt board on the wall. It is one of the strangest things the church has done, to take the most terrifying chapter of judgment in the Old Testament and turn it into wallpaper for toddlers. Read it as an adult and it stops being decoration. The earth is full of violence. God looks at what He made and grieves. And then He acts.

Genesis 6 does not flinch. "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). This is not God reacting to a single scandal. It is the diagnosis of a species, the rot of chapter three spread to fill the world. And the verse that follows is harder still: it grieved Him to His heart that He had made man. The Judge of all the earth is not a cold mechanism processing infractions. He is a wounded Maker.

**Judgment is real, and it is grief before it is wrath**

We would prefer a God too distant to be offended or too soft to act. Genesis gives us neither. The flood is judgment, total and dreadful, the waters of chaos let back over a world that had filled itself with blood. To preach the ark without the water is to preach a rescue from nothing. But notice the order. Before the wrath, the grief. God does not destroy in a rage. He destroys in sorrow, the way a man might weep while he amputates to save a life. The judgment is severe because the wickedness is real, and because the Judge actually loves the world He is judging.

And here I cannot stand outside the indictment with the righteous. The text says every intention of the heart was only evil continually, and that includes the heart I carry into this pulpit. I would like to imagine I would have been on the boat by merit. I would not. The line between Noah and the drowned world is not Noah's goodness. It is grace. "Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord." Favor is not earned. It is found.

**Mercy and judgment meet in one door**

Here is the heart of it. The same flood that drowns the world floats the ark. The very judgment that falls is the thing that lifts the rescued above it. And God does not leave the way of escape vague. He gives Noah exact dimensions, exact materials, and then He gives a door. One door. "You shall make a door for the ark" (Genesis 6:16, paraphrase of the instruction). One way in. Anyone could have come through it while it stood open. The ark was not too small. The door was not too narrow for any who would enter. When the time came, the text says something we often miss: the Lord shut him in. The hand that brought the judgment closed the door of safety. Judgment and mercy meet at one threshold, and the same God presides over both.

This is the offense and the comfort of the gospel held together. There is real judgment, and there is a real door, and the door is not a self-improvement plan. It is a place to stand when the waters come.

**The ark with a door in His side**

Centuries later a carpenter said, "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). The pattern Genesis carved into history finds its person. Christ is the ark, lifted up by the very judgment that should have drowned us, and He is the door, the one way in, thrown open to anyone, narrow enough to exclude no one who comes. On the cross the flood of wrath fell, and He took it, and those who are in Him are carried over it rather than under it.

The rainbow at the end is not sentiment. It is a war bow hung in the sky, pointed away from the earth, a promise written in light that the waters will not have the final word. The God who shut the door also hangs up the bow.

So do not soften this chapter into wallpaper. The water is real. But so is the door, and it is open still.

There is room in the ark.

## The Call of Abram

*Genesis 12*

The story of the world turns on a man we are given almost no reason to admire. We meet him in Ur and then in Haran, a man past seventy with a barren wife and a dead-end family line, a man from a household that, the text later tells us, served other gods. There is no resume here. No record of righteousness that earns what comes next. The God of heaven simply speaks into the silence of an ordinary life and changes the trajectory of human history through it.

The command and the promise arrive together. "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you" (Genesis 12:1). Read what God asks Abram to leave: country, clan, father's house, every source of identity and security an ancient man possessed. And read what God offers in exchange. Not a map. Not a guarantee Abram can hold. A land He will show, later. The call is to walk out of everything certain toward a God who has not yet shown His hand.

**The plan runs through one undeserving man**

Then comes the promise, sevenfold and staggering: "I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:2–3). Stand back and see the scale. After Babel, where men tried to make their own name great and were scattered, God chooses one man and promises to make his name great, to gather what Babel scattered, to bless every family on earth through this single childless nomad. The repair of the whole human race is now riding on one undeserving man.

That phrase matters: undeserving. Nothing in Abram qualifies him. This is the pattern God will keep using and we keep resenting. He does not run His plan through the strong, the deserving, the obvious. He runs it through the barren and the late and the unlikely, so that when the blessing comes no one can mistake its source. The text is careful to give Abram no standing of his own. Everything is gift.

**Blessed in order to bless**

Notice the shape of the promise, because the church forgets it constantly. Abram is blessed, but the blessing does not terminate on Abram. "In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." He is blessed in order to become a blessing. The favor is not a reservoir to hoard. It is a river meant to run through him to the nations. The moment Israel later treated election as a possession to be guarded rather than a gift to be passed on, it betrayed the very call that made it.

And this is where I have to look at my own hands. I am quick to receive grace and slow to be a conduit of it. I want the blessing to stop on me, to make my life comfortable, my name a little larger, my circle a little safer. I will cross an ocean for my own advancement and not cross the street for my neighbor's good. The call of Abram exposes the religion I am tempted to build, a faith curved inward, blessing hoarded behind my own father's house.

**The seed who blesses the nations**

Paul reaches back to this verse and tells us where it was always heading. The promise that all nations would be blessed in Abram was, he writes, the gospel preached beforehand, and the offspring through whom the blessing comes is Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). Abram walked out of Ur toward a land he could not see, trusting a word. Centuries later his greater Son walked toward a cross He could see clearly, so that the blessing promised to one childless man might reach every family on earth, including yours, including the ones you have not yet decided to love.

Which means the question the chapter leaves is not whether you have been blessed. If you are in Christ, you are. The question is whether the blessing is running through you or stopping at you.

Blessed to be a blessing.

## The Mountain and the Lamb

*Genesis 22*

There is no chapter in the Bible I would rather skip. A father, an old man who waited twenty-five years for one promised son, is told to take that son and kill him. We should not rush past how monstrous this sounds. If a man in my church told me God had spoken those words to him, I would not call it faith. I would call for help. The text does not blunt the horror. It sharpens it, naming the boy three times in one sentence: "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love." God knows exactly what He is asking.

And Abraham goes. He rises early, splits the wood, takes the fire and the knife, and walks three days up the mountain with the son of the promise beside him. Three days is a long time to change your mind. He does not. Somewhere on that road the boy asks the question that has haunted every reader since. The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb. And the father gives an answer he could not possibly have understood when he spoke it.

**God provides the sacrifice He requires**

"God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son" (Genesis 22:8). Hold that sentence. The whole chapter hangs on it. Abraham is not announcing a clever escape. He is confessing the deepest logic in all of Scripture, that the God who requires the sacrifice is the God who will supply it. The demand and the provision come from the same hand. Hebrews tells us Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, that he had received Isaac as if from death already and trusted he would receive him again. This is not numbness. It is faith that God's promise and God's command, however they collide, will be reconciled by God Himself.

They reach the place. The altar is built, the wood laid, the boy bound, the knife raised. And at the last possible moment heaven interrupts. "Do not lay your hand on the boy." Then Abraham looks up, and there in a thicket is a ram, caught by its horns. He offers the ram in the place of his son. The substitution is the point. Isaac should have died on that wood. A ram dies instead. The son walks down the mountain alive because something took his place.

**The God who sees, and is seen**

Abraham names the place: "The Lord will provide," and the text adds a line that reaches forward across the centuries, that on the mount of the Lord it shall be provided, or seen. This is not a story about a man passing a cruel test. It is a window cut into the heart of God, showing us how He saves. Not by demanding that we supply what we owe. By supplying it Himself. The lamb is His to give, and He gives it.

Let me be honest about where this lands. I am quick to imagine my faith would hold on that mountain, and slow to surrender the small Isaacs I clutch, the reputation, the security, the plans I have made God promise to bless. Abraham was asked to open his hands on the thing he loved most. I keep mine closed around far less and call it devotion. The chapter exposes how little I actually trust the God who provides.

**The Lamb God did provide**

Where was the ram for the world. Generations later, on a hill that tradition links to that same range, another only Son carried the wood for His own sacrifice up a slope outside Jerusalem. This time no voice cried stop. This time the Father did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, and the substitute on the wood was the Son Himself. John the Baptist would point and say, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). The promise Abraham spoke without understanding was kept in full. God provided the lamb, and the lamb was His Son.

So the chapter I would rather skip turns out to be the gospel before the gospel. Isaac walked down alive because a ram died. You and I walk free because the Lamb did not.

God Himself will provide the lamb.

## Meant for Good

*Genesis 37–50*

The most quoted verse from Joseph's story is spoken by a man who had every earthly reason to say the opposite. Sold by his own brothers. Carried in chains to a foreign country. Lied about, imprisoned for a crime he refused to commit, forgotten by the one man who promised to remember him. By any accounting the ledger of Joseph's life is a record of betrayal. And yet at the end he gathers the brothers who did it to him and says a sentence that reorders the whole story.

The arc takes fourteen chapters because the meaning of it cannot be rushed. A favored boy with a coat and a dream. Jealous brothers who throw him in a pit and sell him for silver. A long descent through Potiphar's house and a prison cell, then a sudden rise to the right hand of Pharaoh, and a famine that drives the very brothers who betrayed him to bow before him without knowing his face. Every thread that looked like ruin is being woven, slowly, into rescue. But here is what the text refuses to do. It never pretends the evil was not evil.

**God's providence does not erase human guilt**

This is where careless comfort goes wrong. We tell suffering people that everything happens for a reason in a way that quietly excuses the people who hurt them. Joseph does not. When he finally speaks the truth to his brothers, he holds two things at once. "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive" (Genesis 50:20). He does not say it was not evil. He says you meant evil. The verb is deliberate. Their intention was real and wicked and theirs. And over the same act, in the same sentence, God had a different intention entirely, aimed at salvation. Two purposes ran through one event. The brothers' was murder. God's was life.

This is the hard, durable comfort Scripture offers, and it is nothing like the cheap version. God does not need your suffering to be secretly good in order to weave good out of it. He does not ask you to call the pit a blessing or the prison a gift. He asks you to believe that no human evil can fall outside His power to redeem it. The sovereignty does not sanitize the sin. It overrules it.

**Forgiveness flows from the long view**

And notice what this conviction produces in Joseph. Not a victim nursing a grievance, not a powerful man taking his revenge, though he had the army of Egypt to do it with. It produces forgiveness. He weeps over the brothers who sold him. He provides for them. "Do not fear," he tells them, "I will provide for you and your little ones." The man with every right to crush them feeds them instead. This is what the long view does. When you believe God was at work even in the pit, you are freed from having to settle the account yourself.

I feel the rebuke in this. I keep short accounts of the wrongs done to me and long accounts of the wrongs I have done. I rehearse my injuries. I would have used the power. Joseph's forgiveness is not weakness or forgetting. It is the fruit of trusting that the One who runs the universe is more committed to redemption than I am to revenge.

**The greater Joseph**

Joseph is a shadow, and the body that casts it comes later. Betrayed by one of His own for silver, handed over to gentile authority, descending into death itself, and raised to the right hand of power to keep a multitude alive, including the very people whose hands were in His betrayal. At the cross the worst intention of men and the saving intention of God met in a single act, exactly as on Joseph's road. They meant it for evil. God meant it for the salvation of the world. And the risen Christ does not return with vengeance for those who put Him there. He returns with bread and forgiveness, saying do not be afraid.

So whatever pit you are reading this from, hold the two truths Joseph held. The evil was real. And it is not the last word.

You meant evil; God meant good.
